passage:
In their small flat in Rotterdam, Elif found the dustpan brush under the sink. Yesterday she had watched Kwame sweep crumbs after dinner. Now she crouched on the kitchen floor, frowning, and pushed the brush in short strokes, just the way he had.
"Swee, swee," she said.
Kwame, drying a plate, stopped and grinned. "You're cleaning?"
Elif nodded seriously and brushed a crumb that wasn't there. Then she held the brush out to him, waiting for his turn.

qa.q: What did Elif find under the sink?
qa.a: She found the dustpan brush.

qa.q: What does Elif's serious frown while sweeping suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels serious and determined about doing the job properly, like a grown-up.

qa.q: How could Kwame support Elif's copying?
qa.a: He could take his turn and then give her small real jobs, like brushing crumbs into the pan together.

qa.q: How might Kwame feel seeing his own movements copied?
qa.a: He likely feels amused and touched, as his grin shows, realising she watches what he does. 😊

grounding: It shows deferred imitation: a toddler copying a household action seen the day before.

passage: I'm Zubin, and my little brother Jatin is two, and he copies everything Dadaji does. Yesterday Dadaji cleared his throat loudly before reading the paper. This morning, Jatin sat on the sofa, held a cushion like a newspaper and went "Hmm-HMM!" in a deep voice. Then he put his hands together and said "Namaste" to the milkman, exactly like Dadaji does at the gate. I don't know if he understands what namaste means. Maybe he just likes the sound. But everyone laughed, and he did it three more times.

qa.q: What did Jatin hold like a newspaper?
qa.a: He held a cushion like a newspaper.

qa.q: What does Zubin think about whether Jatin understands namaste?
qa.a: Zubin is unsure whether Jatin understands it or just likes the sound.

qa.q: How could the family help Jatin learn from this copying?
qa.a: They could greet people warmly in front of him and say the word with him, so the gesture gains meaning.

qa.q: Why might Jatin keep repeating the namaste?
qa.a: Everyone's laughter was a happy response, so he may enjoy the attention and connection it brings.

grounding: An older sibling observes a toddler copying gestures and sounds seen earlier from a grandparent.

passage:
Week one: Jahnavi talked on the phone while cooking. Manoj, eighteen months, watched from the floor.
Week two: Manoj held a wooden block to his ear. "Hallo? Haa?" He nodded, the way his mother did.
Week four: Jahnavi was stirring dal when she heard a clatter. Manoj had a steel bowl and a spoon and was stirring air, very carefully. He even blew on the spoon.
"You're cooking too?" Jahnavi laughed. She gave him a small pot of dry rice to stir.

qa.q: What did Manoj hold to his ear in week two?
qa.a: He held a wooden block to his ear.

qa.q: What does Manoj blowing on the spoon suggest about how closely he watched?
qa.a: It suggests he had noticed small details of his mother's cooking and wanted to do it exactly like her.

qa.q: Which choice by Jahnavi helped when she saw Manoj stirring, and why?
qa.a: She joined in and gave him a small pot of dry rice so his copying became safe, real play.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel seeing her habits come back to her?
qa.a: She probably feels amused and a bit surprised at how much he absorbs, which her laugh shows.

grounding: It shows imitation of household actions developing over several weeks.

passage:
On Tuesday, Mohit, two, watched Dadi ring the little brass bell during evening prayers in their Kolkata flat. Nobody thought he was paying attention.

On Thursday afternoon, Kiran found him in the corner by the prayer shelf. He had a steel spoon in one hand and was shaking it slowly, humming, eyes half closed, just like Dadi. Then he bowed his head so low he nearly toppled over.

Kiran covered her mouth to hide her laugh and called Dadi to come and see.

qa.q: What did Mohit use as a bell?
qa.a: He used a steel spoon, shaking it slowly and humming.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel when she covered her mouth?
qa.a: She felt amused and delighted by Mohit's sweet, funny copy of Dadi, so she hid her laugh and called Dadi to see.

qa.q: How could the family support Mohit's copying?
qa.a: They could invite him to join the prayers, give him a small safe role, and name what he is doing, so his imitation becomes shared learning.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel seeing Mohit copy her?
qa.a: She would probably feel touched and delighted that he noticed and wanted to be like her.

grounding: Shows a toddler copying a household ritual days after watching a grandparent.

passage:
"Hallo? Haan, haan. Okay. Bye!" Arnab, two, held a wooden block to his ear and paced across the room.

Jomon looked up from his laptop. "Who's that you're talking to?"

"Office!" Arnab said, frowning just like his father did.

Jomon laughed. "Is that what I sound like?"

Arnab put the block down, picked up the small broom, and swept the same spot again and again, the way Ammachi did every morning.

"Ammachi, come look, you've got a helper!"

qa.q: What did Arnab hold to his ear?
qa.a: He held a wooden block to his ear like a phone.

qa.q: What does Jomon's question "Is that what I sound like?" suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He seems amused and a little surprised to see himself copied so closely by his son.

qa.q: What could Jomon and Ammachi do with Arnab's interest in helping?
qa.a: They could give him a small broom job of his own and praise his effort, turning copying into a chance to join in.

qa.q: What is it like for Ammachi to see Arnab sweeping like her?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and amused that he has been watching her routine.

grounding: A dialogue shows a toddler imitating his father's phone calls and his grandmother's sweeping.

passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday. Teacher: Francis.
Yesterday afternoon, Gurpreet (two) watched me answer the office phone, holding it between my ear and shoulder while I wrote.
This morning, with no phone in sight, Gurpreet picked up a wooden block, pressed it to his ear, tilted his head to his shoulder and said, “Hallo? Ha. Ha. Okay,” while scribbling on paper with a crayon.
He copied what he saw a day earlier. Next step: a toy phone for the pretend corner.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet press to his ear?
qa.a: He pressed a wooden block to his ear.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet seem to feel while copying the phone call?
qa.a: He seemed absorbed and pleased with himself, busily playing the grown-up role.

qa.q: Why was adding a toy phone to the pretend corner a good idea?
qa.a: It encourages Gurpreet to keep practising the actions he has seen, which is how children learn everyday habits.

qa.q: What would change if Francis had not noticed the pretend call?
qa.a: The chance to support Gurpreet's copying play with a toy phone might have been missed.

grounding: A teacher notes a toddler copying, a day later, the phone gestures he had seen.

passage:
In their courtyard in a village near Nashik, Ganga Aaji swept every morning with a long jhadu, bending low.
The next morning, before Aaji woke, two-year-old Swati found the small hand-broom by the door. She bent low, the way Aaji did, and swept the dust in wobbly circles. She stopped, put one hand on her back, and said, “Oof!”
Aaji came out and burst out laughing. “Who taught you that, my little one?”
Swati swept again, very seriously.

qa.q: What did Swati find by the door?
qa.a: She found the small hand-broom by the door.

qa.q: How did Swati feel as she swept very seriously?
qa.a: She felt proud and important, doing the same grown-up job she had seen Aaji do.

qa.q: How could Aaji support Swati's copying?
qa.a: She could let Swati sweep beside her with the small broom and praise her for helping.

qa.q: How does Ganga Aaji feel seeing Swati copy her?
qa.a: She is amused and delighted, bursting out laughing at the copied “Oof!” 😄

grounding: A toddler copies her grandmother's sweeping, even her gestures, a day after watching it.

passage:
In the week before Christmas, Vera spent an evening in their Madrid flat wrapping presents on the floor, pulling tape with a loud rrrip and pressing it down with two fingers.
The next afternoon, two-year-old Camila found an empty shoebox. She sat on the rug, pulled at nothing, said “Rrrip!” and pressed two fingers carefully on the lid. Then she patted it, just as Vera had.
“Is that for me?” Vera asked.
Camila pushed the box towards her, beaming.

qa.q: What did Camila find the next afternoon?
qa.a: She found an empty shoebox.

qa.q: How did Camila feel when she pushed the box to Vera?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy, pleased to give the present she had “wrapped.”

qa.q: How could Vera build on this game?
qa.a: She could give Camila some paper and child-safe tape to wrap things together.

qa.q: What would change if Vera hadn't asked “Is that for me?”
qa.a: Camila might not have had the chance to finish her play by giving the present, which made the moment feel special for her.

grounding: A toddler copies wrapping actions she saw the evening before during the Christmas season.

passage: I'm Vaibhav, Jeevan's big brother. On Diwali night Dadi lit the diyas, cupping her hand around each flame and saying "Jai ho." Jeevan, who's two, watched from Mummy's lap. The next morning, I found him at the door with an empty diya. He cupped his little hand around it, bent his head and said, "Jai o!" Then he moved to the next one. Nobody had shown him again. I called Dadi, and she laughed so much she had to sit down.

qa.q: What did Dadi say while lighting each diya?
qa.a: "Jai ho."

qa.q: What might Jeevan have been feeling as he copied Dadi the next morning?
qa.a: He likely felt proud and absorbed, playing grown-up.

qa.q: How could Dadi encourage Jeevan's copying safely?
qa.a: She could let him help with unlit diyas and praise his careful hands.

qa.q: How does Dadi react to Jeevan's copying?
qa.a: She is delighted, laughing so much she has to sit down.

grounding: A big brother sees a toddler copy the grandmother's diya-lighting gesture the day after Diwali.

passage:

A week later: Dolma gave her a tiny broom. Zainab swept the doorway, stopped, put a hand on her back just like Dolma did, and sighed.

qa.q: How might Dolma feel seeing Zainab put a hand on her back and sigh?
qa.a: Dolma would likely find it funny and touching, seeing that tired gesture copied.

grounding: Over a week after Losar, a toddler copies a caregiver's sweeping, even her tired gesture.

Hansa peeked. During Navratri the whole family had done the evening aarti. Now two-year-old Sarita stood before the little altar, waving a toy spoon in slow circles.

passage:
In their Istanbul flat, two-year-old Selin picked up the TV remote, pressed it to her ear and paced the hallway. "Evet, evet… tamam," she said in a deep voice, frowning, one hand on her hip.
Her big sister Yara burst out laughing. "That's Baba on the phone last night!"
Selin ended the call with a wave, just as Baba does, then went to the kitchen and started stirring an empty pot with a wooden spoon.

qa.q: What did Selin press to her ear?
qa.a: She pressed the TV remote to her ear.

qa.q: What was Selin probably feeling while copying Baba's phone call?
qa.a: She was probably proud and absorbed, enjoying acting like a grown-up in the family.

qa.q: How could Selin's family encourage this kind of play?
qa.a: They could give her safe toy phones and spoons, join in her pretend calls, and include her in simple kitchen jobs.

qa.q: Why does Yara laugh at Selin's pretend call?
qa.a: Yara laughs because she recognises Baba's deep voice and hand-on-hip pose from last night, and finds the copy funny and sweet.

grounding: Shows a toddler copying gestures and household actions seen earlier, like a parent's phone call and stirring a pot.
